title: A farewell triumph: Capablanca wins gold in Buenos Aires 1939
summary:
Chess Olympiads produce remarkable stories. The 1939 Chess Olympiad in Buenos Aires was particularly dramatic, as Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, while the tournament was still taking place, marking the beginning of the Second World War. Against this backdrop, it is easy to overlook the fact that José Raúl Capablanca, world champion from 1921 to 1927, played his final tournament and his final competitive game in Buenos Aires. | Photo: José Raúl Capablanca (Archive)

In Europe, Germany and Poland were at war with one another; in Buenos Aires, they fought over medals at the chessboard. In the end, Germany finished half a point ahead of Poland to win team gold at a Chess Olympiad for the first and, so far, only time. But the outbreak of war also affected the course of the Olympiad.

Six team matches were not played and were instead recorded as 2-2 draws by default, including Germany v Poland. The English team, which had qualified for the final group, left early. Three of its members, Conel Hugh O'Donel Alexander, Stuart Milner-Barry and Harry Golombek, later worked at Bletchley Park and helped decipher encrypted messages sent by the German armed forces.

But many participants did not return to Europe at all. All five members of the German team, Erich Eliskases, Paul Michel, Ludwig Engels, Albert Becker and Heinrich Reinhardt, remained in South America, while the Polish team also dispersed. Miguel Najdorf and Paulino Frydman stayed in Argentina, and Franciszek Sulik later went to Australia. Savielly Tartakower, however, who had lived in France for years but played for Poland, returned to Europe and joined the Free French forces during the war.

Poster for the Buenos Aires Olympiad | Source: FIDE

For Capablanca, the outbreak of the World War caused hopes of a second World Championship match against Alexander Alekhine, who had gone to the Olympiad as reigning world champion, to fade. Ever since his surprising defeat to Alekhine in the 1927 World Championship match, Capablanca had sought a rematch. In vain, because Alekhine kept finding new reasons not to play him. Instead, he defended his title against Efim Bogoljubow in 1929 and 1934. In 1935, he unexpectedly lost to Max Euwe, who thereby became the new world champion. Euwe, however, gave Alekhine the chance of a return match, and Alekhine took it. He won the 1937 rematch and regained his title.

Alekhine also avoided Capablanca in tournaments. After their 1927 World Championship match, he made sure not to play in the same events as Capablanca. It was not until 1936, nine years after their World Championship match, that they faced each other again at the tournament in Nottingham. Capablanca won. Two further games followed at the 1938 AVRO tournament in the Netherlands. The first was drawn, while Alekhine won the second. It was their last tournament game against each other.

Alekhine (left) and Capablanca during their 1927 World Championship match in Buenos Aires

In Buenos Aires in 1939, however, it was Capablanca who avoided the direct encounter. Capablanca played on board one for Cuba, Alekhine for France, and on 14 September, in the twelfth round of the final group, the two could have faced each other. But Capablanca did not play, so Alberto López Arce appeared on the top board for Cuba against Alekhine and lost in 25 moves. The team match ended 2-2.

Capablanca explained the following day in the Argentine newspaper Crítica that his decision had been made solely for personal reasons. He had already informed the Argentine Chess Federation a week earlier that he would not play against Alekhine. The Olympiad was a team tournament, not an individual event, and neither Cuba nor France were fighting for overall victory.

Nevertheless, Capablanca and Alekhine continued negotiating over a rematch during the Olympiad. On 16 September, Capablanca reiterated in a letter to Augusto de Muro, president of the Argentine Chess Federation, that he was willing to play for the World Championship: "I am ready to play as soon as the match can be organised". Alekhine replied evasively and, in his response of 18 September, pointed out that as a reserve officer in the French army he might be called up for interpreting duties (see Edward Winter, Chess Notes No. 4696 , "Capablanca and Alekhine in Buenos Aires, 1939" ).

In the end, there was never a rematch. The Olympiad did, however, bring Capablanca one final sporting success and a symbolic victory over his great rival. Capablanca remained unbeaten in Buenos Aires and scored 11½ points from 16 games (+7, =9, −0). Alekhine scored 12½ points from 16 games (+9, =7, −0), one point more. Since only the results from the final group counted towards the individual medals at this Olympiad, however, the gold medal for the best performance on board one went to Capablanca. He scored 8½/11 in the final group, while Alekhine had to settle for silver with 7½/10.

This success was Capablanca's swansong. After the Olympiad, he played no more tournaments, only simultaneous exhibitions and casual games. On 7 March 1942, the 53-year-old, who had suffered from high blood pressure for years, had a stroke while visiting the Manhattan Chess Club in New York. He died the following morning at Mount Sinai Hospital.

The last tournament game of Capablanca's life was played at the Buenos Aires Olympiad against the Brazilian Octávio Trompowsky, after whom the Trompowsky Variation 1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5!? is named. Capablanca won the game in the same way he had won countless games throughout his career: he avoided theoretical discussions in the opening, steered clear of tactical complications that might even have favoured him, and instead outplayed his opponent in the middlegame by apparently simple means. This led to a favourable endgame, which Capablanca converted without difficulty.

title: Clutch Chess: Caruana, Nakamura, Sindarov and Pragg meet in Saint Louis
summary:
The Clutch Chess: Champions Showdown event returns to Saint Louis on 27–29 October, with Fabiano Caruana, Hikaru Nakamura, Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu and Javokhir Sindarov (pictured) competing in an 18-game rapid tournament. The four elite GMs will play three double round-robins, with victories worth progressively more points over the three days. A jackpot funded by drawn games further adds entertainment value to the competition. | Photo: Nils Rohde / ChessBase

Sindarov to face elite opposition ahead of World Championship match against Gukesh

The Saint Louis Chess Club will host the Clutch Chess: Champions Showdown from 27 to 29 October, bringing together four chess superstars for an 18-game rapid tournament with a prize fund of $425,000.

Fabiano Caruana, Hikaru Nakamura, Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu and Javokhir Sindarov will compete in an event with an unusual scoring system: wins become increasingly valuable as the tournament progresses, giving players opportunities to make up ground on the final day.

The competition follows the same general format as last year's edition, which was won by Magnus Carlsen. The Norwegian will not defend his title, but Caruana and Nakamura return for another attempt, while Pragg and Sindarov make their first appearances in the event.

The lineup includes the two strongest US players of this era and two young players who have enjoyed considerable success in 2026. Praggnanandhaa won this year's Grand Chess Tour , defeating Caruana in the final back in August, also in Saint Louis. The Indian grandmaster overturned a six-point deficit on the last day of that match to claim the title.

Javokhir Sindarov, meanwhile, won the Candidates Tournament in April and is preparing to challenge Gukesh Dommaraju for the World Championship in November . The Uzbek grandmaster will thus have an opportunity to test himself against three experienced opponents in a rapid event less than a month before his world title match.

Fabiano Caruana recently finished runner-up at the US Championship, losing the title to Wesley So in a rapid playoff after the two players finished level in the classical tournament. Hikaru Nakamura, who remains among the world's highest-rated players despite being mostly inactive, completes the field.

Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu facing Fabiano Caruana at the Grand Chess Tour Finals in Saint Louis | Photo: Lennart Ootes

An unusual scoring system

The four participants will compete in three double round-robins , one on each day. Every player will face each opponent twice per day, once with each colour, for a total of six games daily and eighteen over the tournament.

The time control is 10 minutes per player, with a 5-second increment from move one.

The main feature of the Clutch Chess format, devised by grandmaster Maurice Ashley, is that the value of a victory increases from one day to the next.

Day Win Draw Loss

Day 1 1 ½ 0

Day 2 2 1 0

Day 3 3 1 0

The system gives particular importance to the final six games, when a single victory is worth as much as three wins on the opening day. Moreover, a draw on the last day is worth only one-third of a victory, providing an additional incentive to play for a win.

Javokhir Sindarov was recently in Saint Louis, as he participated in the last two events of the Grand Chess Tour | Photo: Crystal Fuller

According to the tournament regulations , draw offers are not permitted before Black has completed move 60.

The tournament features $425,000 in total prize money, including $125,000 for first place, $94,000 for second, $72,000 for third and $62,000 for fourth. Additional bonuses are awarded for individual victories: $1,000 on day one, $2,000 on day two and $3,000 on day three.

The money allocated to drawn games is accumulated in the Champion's Jackpot , which goes to the eventual tournament winner in addition to the first-place prize. If two players finish tied for first, a single Armageddon game will determine the champion. A three- or four-way tie will be settled by an Armageddon round-robin.

Play begins at 12.00 noon local time (18.00 CET) on Tuesday 27 October, with the same starting time on Wednesday and Thursday. The Saint Louis Chess Club will provide live coverage through its YouTube and Twitch channels, with commentary from grandmasters Maurice Ashley and Yasser Seirawan, alongside broadcaster James Dash Patterson.

Hikaru Nakamura at the Candidates Tournament in Cyprus | Photo: Nils Rohde

Carlsen's victory in 2025

The inaugural edition in October 2025 saw Magnus Carlsen secure overall victory with two games to spare. The Norwegian scored four consecutive wins on the final day, defeating Gukesh and Caruana twice each, and eventually finished with 25½ points.

Caruana took second place with 16½ points, followed by Nakamura on 14 and Gukesh on 10. Interestingly, the Indian world champion had been the sole leader after the opening day, but the increasingly valuable victories allowed Carlsen to pull well ahead in the final stages.
